Hi, Dr. AI. Well, I guess... I mean, I am here because things have been getting a little strange lately. I work as a bookkeeping clerk, you know, doing accounting stuff, mostly data entry and reconciling accounts, which usually I am completely fine at. But recently I have been doing these things at work and at school that just... they do not really make any sense at all. 

Like, the other day, instead of just entering the expenses into the spreadsheet like I am supposed to, I took all the physical receipts. There were probably like fifty or sixty of them from the last month, and I just started lining them up across the floor. End to end, all the way across the carpet. I do not even really know why, I just did it. And then, when I sit at my desk, I have this heavy-duty calculator for my audits, and I have been tapping the keys, but I keep doing it in sets of nine. Just tapping nine times. Over and over. If I lose count, I have to start the set of nine completely over, and it takes up so much of my shift, but I just sit there tapping it. 

But the weirdest part is when I go to make copies. I will go into the copy room, and I just end up standing right by the copier with my hands held up in the air. Just holding them up by my head. And I will stand there like that for who knows how long until someone walks in and asks if I am okay. My supervisor actually walked in on Tuesday and asked what in the world I was doing, and only then did I put my hands down and snap out of it. So, I guess that is why I came in, because I just cannot explain why I am acting like this and it is taking up so much of my day.

Yeah, actually, that has been happening a lot lately. Mr. Henderson, my supervisor, the one I mentioned earlier with the terrible ties, he actually pulled me aside about this just the other day. I was trying to explain to him why this one particular ledger was off by a few hundred dollars. It was supposed to be a simple reconciliation issue, but in my head, there was this whole web of connections that he needed to understand to really get why the numbers were behaving that way.

So, I started out talking about the ledger, right? But then I realized the date on the discrepancy was the exact same date as my tuition deadline for my evening classes. So I started explaining that to him, because the timing felt incredibly relevant to the whole situation. And from the tuition deadline, my brain just naturally went to tax rules, because of the education credits and how they overlap with the quarterly filings we were working on. 

But then, while I was explaining the tax rules, I remembered this specific invoice we had processed for a client who bought all this expensive studio lighting equipment. And I started talking about how the depreciation on the studio lighting tied into those same tax rules, and how the totals on the lighting invoice perfectly matched the number patterns I have been seeing everywhere. The patterns I told you about earlier that are tracking me. 

So I am standing there, trying to lay all this out for him, explaining how the ledger discrepancy, the tuition deadlines, the tax rules, the studio lighting, and the number patterns are all completely connected... and he just put his hands up. He stopped me and said he had absolutely no idea what I was talking about. He told me I was jumping from one completely unrelated idea to another and that he could not follow how I got from a basic ledger error to studio lighting and my tuition. 

And it is so frustrating, you know? Because to me, it makes perfect sense. It is a straight line in my head. Every piece of information leads directly to the next. But when I try to explain it out loud, I guess all the connections get tangled up for other people. They just stare at me. It is not just him, either, a couple of the other clerks have mentioned that my explanations are just too hard to track lately because I jump around too much.

Well, not exactly like I am paralyzed or anything, but... actually, yes, in a way, I do freeze up. I just get stuck doing these bizarre things, like the tapping or the lining things up or standing frozen by the copier, and I don't know why I am doing them, but I just can't seem to stop myself.

No, no, I wouldn't say I am completely unresponsive. It is actually... well, it is kind of the opposite, really. Like I was trying to say a minute ago, if someone says my name or even just makes a loud enough noise, it breaks the whole spell completely.

No, no, nothing like that. I can see why you might ask that, though, like maybe I feel like a puppet on strings or something. But honestly, no. They will be talking about things that I used to absolutely love. We used to go to all these local underground music shows downtown, these really loud, high-energy gigs, or we would get together on weekends and work on these big, messy collaborative art projects. I used to be the one getting everyone hyped up about that stuff. But now, they will be talking about a new band playing this weekend or some new art thing they want to do, and I just feel completely flat inside. I just sit there staring at them. I know I should be smiling or getting excited, but my face just doesn't do anything. I can tell it makes them uncomfortable because I am just giving them this completely reduced, empty expression while they are talking about stuff we used to be so passionate about.\n\nDoctor: When you hold those frozen positions, does someone else ever try to move your arms or legs, and do they stay in that same position afterward?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not really. No one has actually tried to physically grab my arms or move my legs when I get stuck like that. \n\nLike, if we go back to that time in the copy room with Brenda from HR that I was just telling you about... when she walked in and I was just standing there with my hands up in the air by the toner machine. She was just standing there by the door holding this huge stack of manila folders—the thick ones with the reinforced tabs that we use for the end-of-year audits, because she's always running those reports on Thursdays—and she just looked completely confused. You just ask him what he's doing. I don't think they would even get the chance to try, because just the shock of them speaking to me or entering my personal space is usually enough to snap me out of whatever weird holding pattern my brain is stuck in. My ears still work perfectly fine, and my brain processes that someone is talking to me. \n\nIf Brenda at the office says my name, or my roommate asks me a question, or honestly even if a delivery truck honks really loud outside my bedroom window, I snap right back to normal and respond to them. So no, definitely not completely unresponsive. I just need that little external push to get my gears turning again, I guess. And then, of course, I always feel incredibly awkward right after, because I have to act like I wasn't just sitting there like a literal statue. I usually try to play it off, like I pretend I was just deep in thought about an audit report for work or trying to remember a specific tax formula for my evening classes, but I know they probably think it is super weird anyway. But yeah, I always respond when they actually try to get my attention.\n\nDoctor: When you stand with your hands up by the copier, do you feel as if an outside force is making your body do that?\n\nPatient: No, no, nothing like that. I can see why you might ask that, though, like maybe I feel like a puppet on strings or something. But honestly, no. It isn't like some invisible hand is pulling my arms up, or like there's some kind of... I don't know, ghost or magnetic force or mind-control thing happening. It is definitely just me. My own muscles, my own bones. \n\nWhen I am standing there by that copier—the big heavy-duty one on the third floor that always smells faintly like burnt plastic when you run more than fifty pages through it at once—it is entirely my own body doing the action. It's just that I don't understand *why* my body is doing it. That's the part that drives me crazy. Like, I know it is my brain sending the signal to lift my hands up, but I just don't know why it's sending that signal in the first place. \n\nI've actually thought about this a lot. Like, I will be sitting on the bus on my way home from the office—I take the 42 line down past the old shopping center because my car has been making this awful grinding noise in the steering column and I just haven't had the time or the money to take it into a mechanic yet—and I will just be staring out the window, replaying the whole situation with Brenda in my head. And I'll ask myself, 'Did I feel forced? Did someone else make me do that?' And the answer is always no. \n\nThere is no outside pressure, no heavy feeling of someone else guiding my limbs. It is more like... like a glitch in my own programming, if that makes sense. Like my body just decides to hit pause on its own accord and strike this bizarre pose, and my conscious mind is just sort of trapped watching it happen, thinking, 'What in the world are we doing right now?' But it's always me. Just my own confusing, frustrating brain acting up, not any kind of outside force.\n\nDoctor: When you freeze up like that, are you unable to move at all?\n\nPatient: I honestly couldn't tell you if I'm literally unable to move, because... well, because in those moments, the very concept of moving just completely evaporates from my mind. It’s not like I'm fighting against my own body, you know? \n\nIt's not like that sleep paralysis thing. I had a buddy in high school, Jason, who used to get sleep paralysis all the time, and he said it was absolutely terrifying because he would wake up in the middle of the night and try so, so hard to thrash around or yell for his mom, and his body just wouldn't let him do it. He was actively trying to move and couldn't. \n\nFor me, it is nothing like that at all. There is no struggle. When I'm standing by that heavy-duty copier on the third floor, or when I'm staring at the drywall above my peeling particle-board desk, I'm not fighting to put my arms down or turn my head. I'm just... there. The thought of lowering my hands or walking back to my cubicle just doesn't even cross my mind until Brenda says my name or my roommate bumps my chair. \n\nSo I guess I don't really know if I am physically unable to move, because I have never actually tried to break out of it myself while it's happening. It's like my brain just temporarily deletes the instructions for movement, or hits pause on the whole system. My muscles aren't cramped up, I don't feel paralyzed or heavy, but the actual internal command to move just isn't there. So I really can't say for sure if I'm trapped in that position or not, because it never even occurs to me to test the boundaries of it until someone finally snaps me out of it.\n\nDoctor: When you stand frozen like that, do you also become completely mute?\n\nPatient: Well, I guess I am quiet during it, yeah, but I wouldn't say I'm permanently mute or anything because, like I was saying, the second someone actually speaks to me, I answer them right away. But until they do... yeah, I'm not making a peep. Honestly, though, the not speaking part isn't even the main reason I finally decided to come in and see you. I came in because I have started doing all these things at work and school that just do not make any sense whatsoever, and it's really starting to freak me out. \n\nLike, it's not just the freezing up. The other day at work—I'm a bookkeeping and auditing clerk, so I deal with a ton of paperwork and expense reports—I was supposed to be reconciling these travel expenses, and instead of typing them into the system, I just started lining all the receipts across the floor. Just laying them out, end to end, perfectly straight all the way across the ugly gray carpet in my cubicle. I wasn't even reading the amounts on them, just lining them up. \n\nAnd I'll do this weird thing with my calculator, too. I have this really loud, clacky 10-key calculator on my desk for audits, and I will just sit there tapping the keys in sets of nine. Exactly nine taps, over and over again, for no logical reason at all. It makes absolutely no sense. \n\nAnd then, of course, there's the thing we were just talking about, standing by the copier with my hands held up in the air, just completely silent and frozen, until someone finally walks by and asks if I am okay. Once they ask if I'm alright, I can talk perfectly fine again and I put my hands down. So I'm not mute, I just... Yeah, absolutely. It's actually kind of a total 180 from the freezing up thing we were just talking about. It's like... well, it's like a switch flips, and suddenly I have all this buzzing inside my chest and my arms. When that energy comes on, I absolutely cannot sit through a normal bookkeeping shift. I mean, my job is literally just sitting in a chair for eight hours staring at spreadsheets and typing numbers into the system, but when I get like that, sitting still feels physically impossible. It almost hurts to stay seated.\n\nI end up getting up and pacing back and forth in my cubicle—which isn't very big, so it's really just three steps one way, three steps back, over and over again, wearing a path in that same ugly gray carpet I mentioned earlier. I'll just start opening extra tabs on my computer for no reason. Like, dozens of them. I'll have the company portal open, and then I'll open a tab for a web calculator, and then a blank Google sheet, and then a search for office supplies, just click-click-clicking because my fingers can't stop moving. \n\nAnd then I'll look at the physical files on my desk and suddenly decide the entire system is wrong, so I'll start reorganizing files. Brenda actually got really annoyed with me about it last month because she couldn't find the Miller account. But in the moment, I just have so much frantic, nervous energy that I have to be doing *something*, anything, just moving and clicking and sorting at a million miles an hour. It's like I'm driven by this invisible engine and I just can't figure out how to hit the brakes.\n\nDoctor: During those times when you feel unusually energetic and driven to move, do you also feel abnormally euphoric or overly confident?\n\nPatient: Yeah, euphoric is... I mean, confident doesn't even really begin to cover it. It's more like... well, some weeks I just feel unusually sharp, you know? Like my brain is finally operating at a hundred percent capacity and I am just almost completely unstoppable. I'll get home from my evening classes and I won't even be tired. I'll just sit at my particle-board desk in my room and feel like I can map out my entire future in one single night. \n\nI'll start making these massive, incredibly detailed master plans. Because I'm a clerk, right? So I know how to organize data. I'll start charting out exactly how I'm going to finish my degree early, pass the CPA exam on the first try, start my own auditing firm, and make my first million by the time I'm twenty-five. I'll literally make color-coded spreadsheets for my life goals at three in the morning, and I feel so brilliant while I'm doing it. It's like my skin is buzzing and I'm so high up on this pedestal of my own genius that anyone trying to bring me down to earth or correct my work just feels like an absolute insult. I'm trying to get my degree so I can move up from just being a clerk, and I ended up completely bombing this really important course module. I would sit there staring at the textbook, reading the exact same paragraph about asset depreciation over and over again, and absolutely nothing would stick. I'm talking transposed numbers, missing decimal points, assigning expenses to completely wrong department codes—stuff I never used to do. I mean, this is work that used to be so incredibly routine for me. I used to be able to listen to a podcast and knock out twenty expense reports in an hour, no problem. But I just couldn't reliably finish any of it anymore without making these massive mistakes or just losing my train of thought completely. It's just... it's really hard to explain because it doesn't make any logical sense to me either, and I'm a numbers guy, you know? I deal with ledgers and receipts all day, things that have to balance and make sense. But this... this is different. When I get stuck like that at the copier, it's not because my muscles are locked or stiff. It's almost like my brain just forgets how to send the signal to move until someone like Dave or Brenda says something to snap me out of it. \n\nAnd, you know, if you were to come over here right now and physically move my arm... I mean, first of all, it would probably startle me pretty bad. But second of all, I'm pretty sure my arm would just drop right back down to my side, or maybe just go limp. It definitely wouldn't just hover there in mid-air wherever you put it. Because, like I said, the second someone interacts with me, the whole weird spell thing just breaks completely. Gravity takes over again. So no, I don't think it would stay like wax at all. It would just fall back down."
